q: Which neuron is called the final common path to a skeletal muscle?
options: An upper motor neuron in the precentral gyrus
A lower motor neuron in the ventral horn
An interneuron in the dorsal horn
A neuron of the red nucleus

why.correct: Every command to a skeletal muscle, from the cortex, the brainstem or a spinal circuit, must pass through the lower motor neuron, because only its axon leaves the CNS and reaches the muscle fibers.
options: An upper motor neuron's axon stays inside the CNS and ends on lower motor neurons or interneurons. It never reaches the muscle.
Correct. The lower motor neuron is the only route out to the muscle, so it is the final common path.
Dorsal horn interneurons handle incoming sensory signals. They do not send axons to muscle.
The red nucleus holds upper motor neurons of the rubrospinal tract, which end on lower motor neurons in the cord.

q: Put the corticospinal pathway for moving the right hand in order, starting in the brain.
options: Upper motor neuron in the left precentral gyrus
Internal capsule
Pyramid of the medulla oblongata
Pyramidal decussation
Right lateral corticospinal tract
Lower motor neuron in the right ventral horn

why.correct: The upper motor neuron's axon leaves the left precentral gyrus, funnels through the internal capsule, runs in the cerebral peduncle, forms part of the pyramid on the front of the medulla, crosses at the pyramidal decussation, descends in the right lateral corticospinal tract and synapses on a lower motor neuron in the right ventral horn of the cervical enlargement.

q: Roughly what share of corticospinal axons cross at the pyramidal decussation?
options: About 10–15%
About 50%
About 85–90%
Every one of them

why.correct: About 85–90% cross in the lower medulla and form the lateral corticospinal tract. The remaining 10–15% descend uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract, and most of those cross later in the cord.
options: That is the share that does not cross at the decussation: the anterior corticospinal tract.
The split is far from even. The large majority cross in the medulla.
Correct. Most corticospinal axons cross at the pyramidal decussation.
Not every axon crosses here. The anterior corticospinal tract, about 10–15% of the axons, stays uncrossed in the medulla.

q: Blood flow is cut off to a small area of the left internal capsule that carries corticospinal axons. Which side of the body becomes weak?
options: The left side of the body
The right side of the body
Both sides equally
Neither side

why.correct: The internal capsule lies above the pyramidal decussation. The corticospinal axons there have not crossed yet, and they are on their way to cross in the lower medulla and control the right side. Losing them weakens the right side.
options: Same-side weakness follows damage below the pyramidal decussation, in the spinal cord. The internal capsule is above it.
Correct. Damage above the decussation weakens the opposite side.
Each internal capsule carries axons for the opposite side only. Weakness on both sides would need damage on both sides.
The axons of the upper motor neurons pass through the internal capsule. Cutting them stops the signal, even though their cell bodies in the cortex survive.
Lateral corticospinal tract
Anterior corticospinal tract
Spinothalamic tract
Dorsal column

why.correct: The lateral corticospinal tract runs in the lateral white column and carries the crossed corticospinal axons to lower motor neurons for the limbs.
options: Correct. This is the lateral corticospinal tract, in the lateral white column.
The anterior corticospinal tract lies in the anterior column, beside the anterior median fissure.
The spinothalamic tract is ascending: it carries pain and temperature up the cord in the lateral and anterior columns.
The dorsal column fills the posterior column and carries fine touch and position up to the medulla.

misconception: any motor damage makes muscles floppy
q: A limb is weak and floppy, its tendon jerks are absent, its muscles have wasted over six weeks and small twitches ripple under the skin. Where is the damage most likely to be?
options: The primary motor cortex of the opposite side
The internal capsule
The lateral corticospinal tract
The ventral horn or ventral root

why.correct: Flaccidity, lost tendon jerks, marked atrophy and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs. The lower motor neuron's cell body is in the ventral horn, and its axon leaves through the ventral root.
options: Motor cortex damage is upper motor neuron damage. After the first days it produces stiffness and brisk tendon jerks, not wasting with twitches.
The internal capsule carries upper motor neuron axons. Damage there causes spastic weakness of the opposite side.
The lateral corticospinal tract is made of upper motor neuron axons. Cutting it leaves the lower motor neurons healthy, so there are no fasciculations and little wasting.
Correct. These are the signs of a lower motor neuron lesion.

q: Select every finding that points to upper motor neuron damage, weeks after the injury.
options: Spasticity
Fasciculations
Brisk tendon jerks (hyperreflexia)
A Babinski sign
Marked atrophy within weeks
Flaccid paralysis that never changes

why.correct: Upper motor neuron damage frees the lower motor neurons and spinal circuits from descending control: tone rises (spasticity), tendon jerks become brisk and the big toe goes up when the sole is stroked.
options: Correct. Spasticity is raised tone that grows with the speed of stretch.
Fasciculations come from sick lower motor neurons firing by themselves. With upper motor neuron damage the lower motor neurons are healthy.
Correct. Released spinal circuits make tendon jerks abnormally brisk.
Correct. An upward big toe in an adult signals corticospinal damage.
Marked, fast wasting follows loss of the muscle's nerve supply, which is lower motor neuron damage. Upper motor neuron damage causes only slow disuse thinning.
Upper motor neuron damage can cause a floppy limb for the first days or weeks, but it then turns spastic. Lasting flaccidity points to the lower motor neuron.

q: Patient A cannot move the lower right side of her face, but she wrinkles her forehead normally on both sides. Patient B cannot move any part of the right side of his face, forehead included. Which statement explains the difference?
options: A: right facial nerve; B: left motor cortex
A and B: right facial nerve, worse in B
A: left motor cortex or its axons; B: right facial nerve
A: the right motor cortex or its axons; B: the left facial nerve

why.correct: The forehead part of the facial nucleus gets corticobulbar input from both hemispheres, while the lower face part gets it mainly from the opposite hemisphere. Upper motor neuron damage on the left therefore spares the right forehead and weakens only the lower right face. The facial nerve is the lower motor neuron for the whole half of the face, so damage to it weakens everything on that side.
options: This is the reverse. Facial nerve damage weakens the forehead too, and cortex damage spares it.
Sparing of the forehead is not a matter of severity. Any facial nerve damage that weakens the lower face also reaches the forehead, because one nerve supplies both.
Correct. A has an upper motor neuron lesion on the left; B has a lower motor neuron lesion on the right.
The corticobulbar input to the lower face comes from the opposite hemisphere, so right-sided face weakness points to the left cortex, and it points to the right facial nerve, not the left.

q: A knife wound cuts through the right half of the spinal cord at T8. Weeks later, predict the change in each finding compared with before the injury.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the right leg
variables.why: The right lateral corticospinal tract has already crossed in the medulla and carries commands for the right leg, so cutting it at T8 weakens the right leg.

variables.name: Muscle tone and tendon jerks in the right leg
variables.why: The right leg's lower motor neurons below T8 survive but lose descending control, so after the early floppy phase tone and tendon jerks increase.

variables.name: Vibration and position sense in the right leg
variables.why: The right dorsal column carries fine touch, vibration and position from the right side and does not cross until the medulla.

variables.name: Pain and temperature sense in the right leg
variables.why: Pain from the right leg crosses in the cord near where it enters and climbs in the left spinothalamic tract, which is intact.

variables.name: Pain and temperature sense in the left leg
variables.why: Pain from the left leg crosses within a segment or two and climbs in the right spinothalamic tract, which is cut.

variables.name: Voluntary strength of the left leg
variables.why: Commands for the left leg descend in the left lateral corticospinal tract, which is intact.

why.correct: Damage to one half of the cord removes the motor tract and dorsal column for the same side, both of which crossed higher up, and the spinothalamic tract carrying pain from the opposite side, which crossed at entry. The result: same-side upper motor neuron weakness and loss of position sense, opposite-side loss of pain and temperature.

q: Blood flow stops to the arm and face area of the left primary motor cortex, and the neurons there die. Three weeks later, predict each finding compared with before.

variables.name: Strength of the right arm
variables.why: The upper motor neurons for the right arm are in the left precentral gyrus, and their axons cross at the pyramidal decussation.

variables.name: Tendon jerks in the right arm
variables.why: The right arm's lower motor neurons are healthy but lose descending control, so after the early floppy phase their tendon jerks become brisk.

variables.name: Strength of the lower right face
variables.why: The lower face part of the right facial nucleus receives corticobulbar input mainly from the left hemisphere.

variables.name: Strength of the right forehead
variables.why: The forehead part of the facial nucleus also receives input from the right hemisphere, which is undamaged.

variables.name: Strength of the left arm
variables.why: The left arm is driven by the right motor cortex, which is undamaged.

variables.name: Muscle bulk of the right arm
variables.why: Lower motor neurons still supply the muscle, so there is no fast wasting; at most slight disuse thinning over months.

why.correct: Loss of upper motor neurons in the left cortex weakens the right arm and lower right face, with spasticity and brisk tendon jerks appearing over the following weeks. The forehead is spared because of its input from both hemispheres, and muscle bulk is kept because the lower motor neurons survive.

q: A 9-month-old baby's big toe extends upward when the outer edge of her sole is stroked. What does this mean?
options: Damage to her corticospinal tract above the lumbar cord
Damage to the lower motor neurons that supply her toes
A normal finding at her age
Weakness of the muscles that curl her toes downward

why.correct: In infants the corticospinal axons are not yet fully myelinated, so the upward big toe is normal. It changes to the adult downward response by about 1 to 2 years of age.
options: In an adult this would be the Babinski sign of corticospinal damage, but in a 9-month-old it is expected.
Lower motor neuron damage would weaken the toe muscles or remove the response altogether, not produce an upward toe.
Correct. The upward big toe is normal until the corticospinal tract matures.
An upward toe is an active extension, not a failure of the flexors. It reflects the maturity of the descending control, not muscle strength.

q: Which brainstem motor tract drives the antigravity extensor muscles that keep you upright when you start to tip?
options: Tectospinal tract
Vestibulospinal tract
Rubrospinal tract
Anterior corticospinal tract

why.correct: The vestibulospinal tract runs uncrossed from the vestibular nuclei, which receive balance signals from the balance organs deep in the skull, to motor neurons for the extensor muscles of the trunk and legs.
options: The tectospinal tract, from the superior colliculus, turns the head and neck toward a sudden sight or sound.
Correct. Balance signals drive posture through the vestibulospinal tract.
The rubrospinal tract, from the red nucleus, helps drive flexor muscles of the arm and is small in humans.
The anterior corticospinal tract carries voluntary commands from the cortex to neck and trunk muscles. It does not carry the balance signals that correct a tip.

q: In Parkinson's disease, the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra die. Predict each change in the basal nuclei loop.

variables.name: Activity of the direct (go) pathway
variables.why: Dopamine normally excites the direct-pathway striatal neurons, so losing it weakens them.

variables.name: Activity of the indirect (stop) pathway
variables.why: Dopamine normally inhibits the indirect-pathway striatal neurons, so losing it frees them.

variables.name: Inhibition of the thalamus by the globus pallidus output
variables.why: Less direct-pathway inhibition and more indirect-pathway excitation both make the globus pallidus output fire more.

variables.name: Ease of starting a movement
variables.why: A more inhibited thalamus excites the motor cortex less, so movements are slow, small and hard to start.

why.correct: Dopamine favors movement by boosting the direct pathway and damping the indirect one. Without it, the brake from the globus pallidus on the thalamus presses harder, and movement becomes slow and hard to begin.

q: A man's right hand shakes as it nears a cup and he overshoots it, but the hand is still at rest and his grip is strong. Rapidly flipping his right hand over and back is clumsy. Where is the damage most likely to be?
options: The left cerebellar hemisphere
The right cerebellar hemisphere
The left substantia nigra
The right lateral corticospinal tract

why.correct: Intention tremor, overshooting (dysmetria) and clumsy rapid alternating movements with normal strength are cerebellar signs. Cerebellar damage shows on the same side, and the lateral hemisphere handles skilled limb movement, so the right cerebellar hemisphere is the likely site.
options: The cerebellum's output crosses and the corticospinal tract crosses back, so each side of the cerebellum coordinates the same side of the body. Left cerebellar damage would affect the left hand.
Correct. Same-side cerebellar signs with normal strength point here.
Substantia nigra damage causes a tremor at rest and slowness, not a tremor that grows near a target.
Cutting the corticospinal tract causes weakness. His grip is strong.

q: Name the pinned region of the cerebellum.
options: Vermis
Cerebellar hemisphere
Flocculonodular lobe
Middle cerebellar peduncle

why.correct: The vermis is the narrow midline strip joining the two cerebellar hemispheres. With the strip beside it, it forms the spinocerebellum, which controls posture and corrects movement as it happens.
options: Correct. This is the vermis.
The hemispheres are the large lateral parts on either side of the vermis.
The flocculonodular lobe is the small lobe on the underside: a nodule in the midline and a flocculus on each side.
The peduncles are white matter stalks connecting the cerebellum to the brainstem, not a region of the cerebellar surface.

q: This sequence describes how the direct pathway of the basal nuclei lets a chosen movement go ahead. Which step is wrong?
options: The motor cortex excites direct-pathway neurons of the striatum
The striatal neurons inhibit the output neurons of the globus pallidus
The globus pallidus output now inhibits the thalamus more strongly
The thalamus excites the motor cortex, and the movement goes ahead

why.correct: The globus pallidus output is itself inhibitory and fires all the time. When the striatum inhibits it, it fires less, so the thalamus is inhibited less, not more. Removing that brake frees the thalamus to excite the cortex.
options: This step is right. Cortical input to the striatum is excitatory.
This step is right. Direct-pathway striatal neurons are inhibitory and act on the globus pallidus output.
This is the error. An inhibited globus pallidus inhibits the thalamus less: the brake is released.
This step is right. A released thalamus excites the motor cortex.

q: Fill the gap in the cerebellum's input and output routes: signals from the spinal cord enter through the inferior cerebellar peduncle → the cortex's motor plan, relayed by the pons, enters through ______ → corrections leave through the superior cerebellar peduncle toward the thalamus.
options: The internal capsule
The corpus callosum between the hemispheres
The cerebral peduncle of the midbrain
The middle cerebellar peduncle

why.correct: The middle cerebellar peduncle, the largest, joins the pons and carries the relayed copy of the cortex's motor plan into the cerebellum.
options: The internal capsule is a band of axons deep in each cerebral hemisphere, not a connection of the cerebellum.
The corpus callosum joins the two cerebral hemispheres to each other.
The cerebral peduncles are stalks on the front of the midbrain that carry the corticospinal axons down. They do not enter the cerebellum.
Correct. The middle peduncle carries input from the pons.

q: A 58-year-old has wasting and twitching of the muscles of both hands, yet his knee jerks are brisk, both big toes go up when his soles are stroked, and sensation is normal everywhere. What best explains this mixture?
options: Damage to the dorsal columns of the cord
Damage to both upper and lower motor neurons
Damage to one cerebellar hemisphere
Damage to the peripheral nerves of both arms

why.correct: Wasting and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs; brisk tendon jerks and Babinski signs are upper motor neuron signs. Normal sensation means the sensory pathways are spared. A disease that destroys both kinds of motor neuron, such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, produces exactly this mixture.
options: Dorsal column damage would remove vibration and position sense, and sensation here is normal.
Correct. Both motor neuron types are affected, and sensation is spared.
Cerebellar damage causes clumsiness with normal strength and no wasting, twitching or Babinski sign.
Damage to the arm nerves would explain the hands, but not the brisk knee jerks and upward toes, and it would usually affect sensation too.
Pyramidal decussation
Cerebral peduncle
Anterior corticospinal tract
Internal capsule

why.correct: At the junction of the medulla and spinal cord, most corticospinal axons cross the midline in the pyramidal decussation (the decussation of the pyramids) and continue as the lateral corticospinal tract.
options: Correct. This is where most corticospinal axons cross.
The cerebral peduncle is higher up, on the front of the midbrain.
The anterior corticospinal tract is the uncrossed bundle running down beside the anterior median fissure of the cord.
The internal capsule lies deep in the cerebral hemisphere, well above the medulla.
